subject: art-design
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In drawing, what does the term 'hatching' refer to?
options: A series of closely spaced parallel lines used to build up tone
Rubbing the surface to lift out highlights
Drawing only the outline of an object
Smudging graphite with a finger to blend
questions.explain: Hatching creates tone and the illusion of form by drawing sets of roughly parallel lines close together.

questions.q: Which set lists the three primary colours?
questions.explain: The primary colours in painting are red, yellow and blue, from which the secondary colours are mixed.

questions.q: Mixing blue and yellow paint together produces which secondary colour?
questions.explain: Blue and yellow combine to make green, one of the three secondary colours.

questions.q: A tint of a colour is created when you add which of the following?
questions.explain: Adding white to a colour lightens it and produces a tint.

questions.q: A shade of a colour is produced by adding which of the following?
questions.explain: Adding black darkens a colour to create a shade.

questions.q: Which of the following is a formal element of art?
questions.explain: Tone is one of the formal elements (line, shape, form, tone, texture, colour and pattern); composition, proportion and perspective are not.

questions.q: In linear perspective, the point on the horizon line where receding parallel lines appear to converge is called the:
questions.explain: Parallel lines in linear perspective appear to meet at a vanishing point on the horizon line.

questions.q: Complementary colours are best described as colours that:
options: Sit opposite each other on the colour wheel
Sit next to each other on the colour wheel
Are made only by adding white
questions.explain: Complementary pairs, such as red and green, lie opposite one another on the colour wheel and create strong contrast.

questions.q: In a painting, warm colours such as red and orange tend to:
options: Appear to advance towards the viewer
Appear to recede into the distance
questions.explain: Warm colours generally seem to come forward, while cool colours appear to recede.

questions.q: An artist uses a range of tones from light to dark in an observational study mainly in order to:
questions.explain: Careful tonal variation describes light and shadow, giving objects a convincing sense of solid, three-dimensional form.

questions.q: In a drawing, 'negative space' refers to:
options: The space around and between the objects
The darkest tones in the composition
questions.explain: Negative space is the area surrounding and between objects, and observing it helps achieve accurate shapes and proportions.

questions.q: The watercolour technique known as 'wet-on-wet' involves:
options: Applying wet paint onto a wet surface to create soft, blended edges
Painting onto dry paper to produce crisp, sharp edges
Dragging an almost dry brush across the paper
Scratching lines into fully dried paint
questions.explain: Wet-on-wet lets colours bleed and merge into soft, diffused edges, useful for skies and backgrounds.

questions.q: Compared with acrylic or oil paint, watercolour is characteristically:
options: Transparent, allowing the white of the paper to show through
Impossible to build up in layers
questions.explain: Watercolour is a transparent medium, so lightness comes from the paper showing through thin washes rather than from white paint.

questions.q: The formal element 'texture' is best described as:
options: The surface quality of a work, how it looks or feels
The lightness or darkness of an area
The path traced by a moving point
The amount of space an object occupies
questions.explain: Texture describes surface quality, which may be actual (physically felt) or visual (implied through mark-making).

questions.q: You want to deepen a shadow in a painting without it looking flat or muddy. A good approach is to:
options: Mix in a little of the colour's complementary
Add a large amount of black
questions.explain: Adding a touch of the complementary colour darkens and neutralises a hue while keeping it lively, avoiding the deadness of straight black.

questions.q: To build up thick, raised strokes with visible brush or palette-knife marks, an artist would use which technique?
questions.explain: Impasto applies paint thickly so that the marks stand up from the surface, adding texture and energy.

questions.q: When drawing an arm pointing directly towards you, the technique used to show it appearing compressed and shortened is called:
questions.explain: Foreshortening depicts an object receding towards the viewer as visually compressed, following the rules of perspective.

questions.q: To make a distant hill appear further away in a landscape painting, an artist could paint it using:
questions.explain: Atmospheric perspective makes distant objects appear cooler, paler and less detailed, so muted blue-greys suggest depth.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Art and Design specifications; Drawing and Painting
